subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-REMOVAL OF COAT OF ARMS FROM PUBLICATION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege in connection with the publication of the standing orders of the House of Commons in January, 1969. It will be noted that in a provisional reprint of the rules published in 1966, the coat of arms appeared on the standing orders. In 1967 a further reprint was made, again with the coat of arms thereon. The reprint that has been delivered to members of the House of Commons has had removed therefrom the coat of arms and for it has been substituted the Speaker's chair.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-REMOVAL OF COAT OF ARMS FROM PUBLICATION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-REMOVAL OF COAT OF ARMS FROM PUBLICATION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am
amazed to see the degree to which there is approval by members of the cabinet of this surreptitious act. I would ask, because this took place during your absence while visiting India, who made the decision for the removal of the coat of arms? The number of ministers who have applauded would indicate that what was done must have come about through the action of the cabinet; otherwise they would not have been applauding an act that cannot be justified outside parliament. As a member of this house I take the strongest objection to steps being taken by this government, outside parliament and parliamentary decision, to bring about a severance of our traditions. If changes are to be made they must be made by parliament and not by cabinet or by certain cabinet ministers.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-REMOVAL OF COAT OF ARMS FROM PUBLICATION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-REMOVAL OF COAT OF ARMS FROM PUBLICATION OF STANDING ORDERS

This trend has been going on for some time, and I am surprised that it apparently receives the support of the cabinet, if one is to judge by the earlier applause of cabinet ministers. I ask Your Honour to look into this matter, and once and for all put an end to the erosion of our traditions in this country by the actions of a government that
will not bring these matters before parliament but act under the table.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps it might be of assistance to the house to make a brief announcement in respect of the proposed business for the coming week. We propose to begin on orders of the day today with the four bills relating to pesticides, pest control and animal contagious diseases; the four pieces of legislation in the name of the Minister of Agriculture. These bills are closely related one to the other in administrative structure, and it is felt they could be most effectively dealt with as a group by the standing committee on agriculture. It is the government's hope that they might be given early passage at the second reading stage so that they might receive more intensive consideration in committee. Following committee study, a more informed opinion would be possible as to the amount of time to be taken to deal with them on the report stage and third reading.
The order we propose for calling the items would be as follows: Nos. 19, 18, 20 and 43. Following those items we would ask that government order No. 7 be called, second reading of the act to amend the Farm Machinery Syndicates Credit Act. In view of the fact that the measure was extensively debated earlier in the session, we hope that it too would receive rapid passage at the second reading stage.
January 14, 1S69

The next item would be No. 25, the legislation with reference to the Bretton Woods Agreement Act and related statutes. The intention would be that the bill be referred to the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs for a more detailed study. The next item to be called would be government order No. 30, second reading of the legislation to establish the fresh-water fish marketing corporation. The motion proposes reference of the bill to the standing committee on fisheries and forestry. It is anticipated that interested persons from western Canada concerned with the industry will want to make representations to the committee with respect to the bill. In view of the debate on the general subject matter which has already taken place, it is not anticipated that debate on the second reading stage would be too extended.
The next item would be No. 13, for second reading of an act to amend the Patent Act, the Trade Marks Act and the Food and Drugs Act, that is to say, the drug prices bill, which would be referred to the standing committee on health, welfare and social affairs. On Thursday I expect to be in a position to make the customary announcement with respect to further business for the balance of this week and for next week.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to announce the licensing for sale in Canada of Pitic 62, a wheat variety which was bred in Mexico. In the interest of brevity I would request permission to table copies of a press release which sets out details of this action taken by the Department of Agriculture today. The house will appreciate that important segments of the grain industry have expressed considerable interest in making a wider range of wheat classes available to farmers. This variety is of a different class and has the advantage of being higher yielding, but it is distinctly inferior in milling and baking qualities to our own milling wheats. Details about seed supplies, grades, etc., are outlined in the documents that I hope to table.
Grain
In conclusion, I think it cannot be overemphasized that because of its inferior baking and milling qualities, this class of grain, while it is called wheat, is not wheat in the sense that it will be allowed entry into the marketing channels that are normally considered for wheat in Canada today.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to hear the last statement of the Minister of Agriculture because in the news release, which is in much greater detail-the minister did not read it-the Board of Grain Commissioners advises that, because of its inferior quality, Pitic 62 would only be eligible for grading into the feed grades of wheat. So it does not mean anything in the way of assisting in developing a new variety of wheat that might be more acceptable than our high protein variety sold in the markets of the world.
I would be more interested if at this stage the minister was looking into the matter of the four or five idle ships waiting in the docks of Vancouver for dry wheat. The government should be doing something to get the grain to these ships.
Probably if the Prime Minister at the Commonwealth prime minister's conference had been flirting a little more with markets than with skirts the farmers would have been better off.

Mr. Speaker, grain and livestock farmers are of course always looking for good wheat grain varieties to raise, and better varieties are still needed, but I suggest, sir, that this hardly can be called a variety that is to any great degree better than those we now have. It may be that in the future our experimental stations will crossbreed this grain to bring a higher yielding feed grain than we have now. However the shortcomings that the minister specified in his announcement points to the fact that this grain is hardly worthy of mention in this house and is hardly worth getting excited about. There may be parts of the prairie provinces, or certain sections of Ontario, where this grain can be raised, and it may be that Quebec and the maritimes may be able to use this variety-I do not know; the minister has not said. It is subject to smut and bunt and other crop diseases, which is hardly an additional asset to the grain industry in Canada. So I hope the minister will see

maintopic: EFFORTS TO AVOID INTERRUPTION OF POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I am surprised that the letter carriers union should have criticized implementation of the five-day week. At its last annual convention the union passed a resolution calling for the early implementation of the five-day week. This measure was also recommended by the Montpetit commission of inquiry. It is being implemented both to achieve cost savings- and these are in the order of $13 million-and to improve working conditions.

Secondly, Mr. Speaker, I am surprised that the union deemed it advisable to state that they had not been advised of this change before January 2.
The first letters announcing the changes in detail were sent to the union by the assistant deputy minister on October 3.
Later on, in October, November, December and during the first week of January, 13 exchanges occurred between the officials of the department and the union representatives either through correspondence or meetings.
Some of these meetings were held last week and even this morning. I am ready to meet the union leaders at any time, if necessary, and I told them so right from the very first meetings which took place in my office.

I am also surprised that the union should have stated that the coincident move on February 1 to a new system of letter carrier delivery represents a retrograde step for the employees or for the public. The cost saving of this move is approximately $3 million, which represents a significant saving to the Canadian taxpayer.
This new system differs significantly from the old straight-line or straight-through delivery criticized by the union. Under that system letter carriers left the post office in the morning and continued on their walk, on occasion eating their lunch on the way, until they had completed their deliveries. Under the new
January 14, 1969

system of non-return delivery, letter carriers, after completing their morning round, will be provided with free transportation to the nearest post office, to their home or to a restaurant, whichever they prefer. The difference lies in the fact that under the new system they will no longer return to the post office to sort letters for afternoon delivery.
Now, what is involved? An average of about 20 first class letters are sorted on each day for delivery in the afternoon. Considering the time involved, I do not consider this procedure economic. The effect upon householders is that these 20 or fewer first class letters will be delivered the following morning instead of that afternoon. This represents 20 first class letters of which, on the average, at least three quarters are business mail, such as bills, divided among the 150 points of call on that afternoon walk.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
On the issue raised by the union of lay-offs as a result of the five day week, here are the facts. A total of 2,068 positions will become redundant as a result of these changes. To take care of these employees we stopped all hiring as of last October 1. As a result, alternative positions at the same salary have been found for all but 601 of the more than 2,000 employees affected. We have in hand another 215 unfilled vacancies. This leaves us 386 positions. To take care of these we intend, and have so informed the union, that all persons in redundant positions will be maintained on strength for 60 days after February 1. As a result of normal retirements this should open up a considerable number of other vacant positions. At the end of that 60 days we will discuss with union officials any unresolved cases and settle those to the satisfaction of both parties concerned.
Finally, I should like to say this. The post office is undergoing radical change. The public is underwriting that change to the extent of some $90 million a year in increased rates. Post office employees have secured, and rightly so, major wage increases in the past few years. The five day week is being implemented, as I said, to improve working conditions. I invite unions to co-operate with us in achieving a common goal-a better, more efficient post office which serves the public better and which is, by no means least of all, a better place to live and work in.

maintopic: EFFORTS TO AVOID INTERRUPTION OF POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we all want an efficient postal service in Canada. I asked my question because many people want some
Inquiries of the Ministry assurance that the Postmaster General and the government generally will make an earnest, sincere and reasonable effort to ensure there is no interruption of service. There is a widespread feeling in the country, and I myself have shared in that, that the prolonged strike last summer was unnecessary, and the result of the government's failure to bargain and discuss questions in good faith until the strike commenced.
I am not rising today to speak for the union; that is not my business, nor is it my place to do so. The members of the union are quite capable of speaking for themselves. Nevertheless I am not exactly comforted by what I interpret as the righteous attitude this afternoon of the Postmaster General.

maintopic: EFFORTS TO AVOID INTERRUPTION OF POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: The self righteous attitude.

maintopic: EFFORTS TO AVOID INTERRUPTION OF POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: He expressed surprise at this and surprise at that; he expressed surprise at the reaction of the union. If one wishes to talk about surprise it must be noted that a good many Canadian people are rather surprised at the quality of the mail service existing at the present time. I hope the Postmaster General will bear in mind, as I am sure he will, that while it is all very well to talk about savings you do not save very much unless you have a willing and co-operative work force. I did not rise to lecture the Postmaster General but merely to express the hope that these grievances will be discussed in good faith with a view to reaching a genuine and satisfactory solution which will preserve the working conditions of the men concerned, and will ensure the Canadian public of good postal services that will not be interrupted by any unnecessary stoppage of work.

speechtext:
It
was obvious as one listened to the Postmaster General that, like the Prime Minister, he has learned Marshall McLuhan's message very well:	You can say one thing and mean
another.
On a number of occasions both inside and outside the house the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) endorsed the basic principles of the Freedman report, that workers shall be consulted and that workers shall not suffer as a result of technological changes. Yet here we have an illustration of government thinking. It is clear that a great number of workers will be laid off as a result of the government's decision to implement the five day delivery. On a number of occasions the Postmaster Genera] made clear and precise statements

January 14. 1969
Inquiries of the Ministry that not a single postal worker would be laid off because of the new system. The remarks are in Hansard, Mr. Speaker, although this is not the time to read them. The minister knows he made those statements, yet today he can only say that at some time six months from now, if there are postal workers for whom positions have not been found, the government is prepared to discuss that matter with its employees.
I can only say, Mr. Speaker, that either the minister lied when he made the statement that no one would be laid off, or he has changed his mind. Now the minister says this new system means there will be a better service. He said that when a post office worker went back to the post office he picked up only 30 new letters for delivery, of which two thirds may have been bills. Now, none of us like getting bills, but the fact is that the 30 letters we are speaking of were delivered on the same day they were received in the post office. Under the new system they will not be delivered until the next day.
The minister says the department is going to save money and it will be more efficient. Of course he is talking nonsense and I am sure he knows it. He said arrangements will be made to pick up letter carriers at noon to take them back to the post office or to some place where they can eat lunch. This is something new. That decision could not have been discussed with post office workers two days ago, because when I was in Winnipeg last week I met postal workers who are delivering mail and that matter was not mentioned. He said: Mr. Speaker, it is my proposal that four bills, C-155, the pesticide residue compensation bill, C-154, the plant quarantine bill, C-156, amending the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, and C-157, the pest control products bill, be considered by the house together. The reason for this suggestion is that they are very much interrelated. The first three mentioned all make provision for compensations to primary agricultural producers in certain situations and the first contains a general provision creating an opportunity for producers to appeal the level of compensation awarded. The fourth bill, C-157, deals with pesticides, as does the first one.
The pesticide residue compensation bill provides for appeals against compensation awarded under this new act as well as under other acts to which these appeal provisions are also applicable. These appeal provisions are made applicable to the plant quarantine bill and the Animal Contagious Diseases Act

by the bills presented. There is, therefore, very good reason for considering these four measures together.
I should like to repeat the suggestion made by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) that all these bills be referred to the standing committee on agriculture for detailed consideration clause by clause.
To refer to the specific bills, Bill C-155 has reference to the proposed pesticide residue compensation act. As is well known to all hon. members, pesticides have become an integral part of our food production picture, as well as having a multiplicity of uses around the home, in the garden, in public recreation areas and indeed in many of our industries. We just could not economically produce some of our important crops without pesticides.
I suppose that most of us dream of the day when pesticides will no longer be required. Agricultural scientists are striving to come up with alternatives to these control materials and are having some measure of success, but the promised land is not yet in sight so far as doing without some of these very useful chemicals in the production of agricultural products is concerned.
Pesticides are rendering a magnificent service to agriculture and, indeed, to the public at large, but from time to time in spite of careful research and testing the use of pesticides in accordance with recommended practice leads to a residue remaining in food that renders the sale of the food in violation of the Food and Drugs Act.
To protect the public interest we have some very stringent requirements concerning the use of these potentially dangerous materials. Our rules are especially strict in regard to pesticide residues in food. The sale of agricultural products containing even minute quantities of residue can be banned under the Food and Drugs Act. This can work a real hardship on an individual farmer because not only does he lose the immediate revenue from his produce but contamination may be such that future marketings may also be affected.
The pesticide residue compensation bill is designed to assist farmers who suffer losses because of pesticide residue through no fault of their own. More specifically, this bill provides the Minister of Agriculture, through the governor in council, with authority to pay compensation to farmers for losses resulting from pesticide residues in food products which are withheld from sale as a result of action under the Food and Drugs Act.
January 14, 1969	COMMONS
Eligibility for compensation is dependent on the residues not having occurred through the fault of the farmers. Also, the use of the pesticide must have been in accordance with recommendations made, approved or concurred in by the Canada Department of Agriculture.
Passage of this bill will restore confidence to those farmers who wish to use pesticides according to directions in the economic production of crops and who may have felt some uncertainty because of the significant losses experienced by a very few farmers as a result of pesticide residues. In framing this act the aim has been to make it as easy as possible for the farmer to establish his eligibility for compensation and the amount of compensation while at the same time not interfering with the normal rights and responsibilities of farmers and, indeed, manufacturers of pesticides.
The bill also provides for the appointment of assessors to hear appeals from compensation awards. The powers of the assessors are binding and provide for confirming or varying the decision of a minister and referring cases back to the minister for such further action as may be necessary. Perhaps I should also add that any producer of primary agricultural products will be eligible for compensation.
Pesticide residues include residues of all pest control products such as insecticides, fungicides, herbicides and fumigants. The bill provides that compensation may not be paid until steps have been taken by the farmer to reduce the amount of loss and to pursue any action the farmer has in law against the manufacturer of the pesticide, or any other person.
The provisions I mentioned earlier for appeals against levels of compensation paid under this act may be made to apply to other acts where provisions are made in such other acts for their application. There are two other acts which will be dependent upon or referred to in the provisions of this act in so far as compensation and appeals from amounts of compensation are concerned. It might be well for me to point out at this stage that the financial consideration would not amount to more than $100,000 annually. This is based on our experience. Indeed, the amount may be substantially less because we must find a situation in which in fact the food and drug directorate has banned the sale of some product before the farmer would become eligible. It must also be established that the residue of these chemicals got into the food through no

Mr. Speaker, I express my thanks to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) for his co-operation in this regard. We would rather deal with these bills one at a time because there are definite principles involved in each of them to which we would like to give very serious consideration. My remarks this afternoon will not be at great length because I believe there is general agreement among all members that legislation of this type is and has been needed for some time, perhaps ever since the extensive use of chemicals in the control of diseases and insects that affect crops which provide human and animal food began.
Having considered the terms of the bill and listened to the explanatory remarks of the minister, I believe there is a strong feeling in the house that the basic issue we must always keep before us is the health of animals and humans who consume food produced from the soil on farms where chemicals are being used. We must consider, on the other hand, that in view of the conditions under which food is produced at the present time we in fact need not only the chemicals we now have but new chemicals to control the various pests and

Pesticide Residue Compensation diseases that from time to time affect farm production.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I think the minister is right in his contention that the government will not have to spend great sums of money in implementing this legislation because I believe that under the provisions of the bill there is very little recourse for a farmer to obtain redress when his crops are condemned because they are contaminated by pesticide residue. It seems to me that before an individual can present a claim to the government he must on his own initiative exhaust all other courses open to him. He must exhaust all avenues of approach, including the companies which provided the chemicals and the custom operators who applied them to his property or adjacent properties. Therefore it appears that once more the onus has been placed on the primary producer, the farmer. Not only is he faced with the loss of the sale of his products, which may be reduced greatly and in extreme cases may be barred from the market completely, but he is faced with the additional expense of making a claim or pursuing an appeal through the various avenues open to him.
There is one other matter that I think should be, and perhaps will be, explored when this bill is referred to the standing committee on agriculture. I was very pleased indeed to hear the minister emphasize over and over again that it was the intention of the government to refer the bill to the committee. This will give an opportunity to those members of the house directly interested in the subject, and the various experts, companies and individuals concerned with this question, to go into the matter in a very thorough and exact manner in order that the farmers of this country, the primary producers, will have the very best possible bill that it is in our power to enact.
I believe that one of the main problems we should be attacking as a group vitally interested in the welfare of this generation and generations to come concerns the type and composition of the chemicals that are applied to the land. We sometimes find that the application of chemicals to crops can create greater problems because of their residue or action than those which it is sought to control. I speak of chemicals that do not after application break down or change their form in any manner and are therefore a constant threat to the environment in which they are

used. They may be a constant threat to animals because of their presence in the topsoil of the land to which they are applied. They may be a constant threat to fresh-water and, indeed, salt-water fish because these chemicals are sometimes carried away through soil drainage to our rivers and lakes and thus to the ocean. Some of the chemicals used lodge in the bodies of the insects they are intended to control and thus are a real threat to various species of bird life of which we in this country are so proud.
My primary point in asking the minister to deal with each of these bills separately was that although they are related in that they deal with chemicals the principles involved are of such magnitude and the ramifications are so great that I believe we must have an opportunity to express our views in regard to each of them. In principle we believe that the action of the government in introducing this bill is commendable. When reviewing the bill we would like an opportunity to deal with each of the clauses in a very explicit manner. In particular we would like from the government explanations of the regulations set out in the bill. After considering the bill I am of the opinion that although its specific purpose is to provide compensation to farmers, the manner in which the bill is drafted means it will be almost impossible for farmers to receive extensive redress for damage. In fact, if they are able to receive compensation it will only be after a long and costly dialogue with the government and the other parties concerned. In the course of our review of the bill we might find a much swifter method of resolving matters as between the injured parties, the farmers, and the government. It is my hope that we shall be able to do this.
We in this party will endeavour in the consideration of these bills to pay every attention to safeguarding the welfare of the people and the animals that consume the production of our soil. Second, we shall investigate these chemicals thoroughly to ascertain whether or not they will remain as active agents in the years ahead. Third, we shall do our very best on behalf of the farmers to make sure that when this legislation becomes law it will be in the most workable form possible.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks made by the minister and by the speaker for the official opposition. I must say that Bill C-155 is a very important piece of legislation and it is my hope that it is just the start of a series of

legislative changes regarding the use of pesticides. While this bill deals with compensation to farmers whose agricultural products have been contaminated by pesticide residue it nevertheless leaves much to be desired in the field of control, something that the house must look at very carefully in the months to come. This bill can be described as legislation to provide compensation to those farmers whose products have become contaminated by the use of government approved pesticides. Basically this is the content of the legislation before us.
While I agree with the preceding speaker that legislation of this type is certainly long overdue I believe that compensation for loss is only one facet of the problem. I feel it is imperative that the Department of Agriculture in conjunction with other government departments do far more research into the possible effects of pesticides before they are released for public use. I find it rather disconcerting to realize that over the years we have been using pesticides which in many instances have contaminated the soil and the products grown in it. There is not doubt that this type of soil pollution is extremely widespread not only in this country but in every country in the world. The relatively few cases of this type of pollution which becomes public knowledge are only a fraction of those which really take place. However perhaps the most disconcerting aspect of the pesticide problem is the fact that government agencies have approved their use only to find out later that very severe contamination has taken place.
I would be the first to admit that pesticides are certainly required in the agricultural industry. In British Columbia there are many kinds of farms and pesticides are certainly required to control some pests. In the past one of the problems has been the lack of proper co-operation between the federal and provincial departments of agriculture. It seems to me that in many instances of problems of pollution of agricultural products there has not been the proper degree of coordination and co-operation between the provincial and federal departments concerned.
I can think of a case which took place several years ago in Grand Forks. I am quite certain that the minister and his department are well aware of the problem that arose when contamination took place and the farmers concerned were placed in an extremely awkward financial position. They had been raising milk cows and sending their milk to the creamery. Contamination was discovered,
Pesticide Residue Compensation and very naturally and logically the creamery had to refuse to take the product. For at least two years a great fight went on, first with the provincial member for the Grand Forks district and then with the department of agriculture of British Columbia. Finally the matter reached the federal field and eventually partial compensation was received by the farmers who had the contaminated product. I think this is a good case to illustrate the point that research facilities are needed desperately in this field.
The above problem in regard to pesticides arose initially because of the use of a pesticide called Aldrin which was used to spray potatoes, I understand. Once Aldrin gets into the soil it often converts itself into a more toxic pesticide called dieldrin. This is the pesticide that caused the problem in the area to which I referred. It did not occur in the crop for which it was used but was found several years later in the hay which cattle had been eating. It took months to search for and find the source of this contamination.
It seems to me that we in Canada have been far too hasty in giving the green light to the use of certain types of pesticides without thoroughly investigating the results which might occur because of a particular pesticide coming into contact with something in the ground and becoming more toxic. We are the only ones that can be blamed. We have allowed this to take place. I am not saying that one government has been more negligent than another, but certainly once these problems are pointed out we should make sure that legislation to protect against this type of problem is placed upon the statute books of our country.
There are one or two more points I should like to make about the use of pesticides. I must say I am very pleased to see a clause in the bill which gives the minister, before paying any compensation to a farmer, the right to insist that the crown be allowed to sue the manufacturer. At least, that is how I interpret the legislation; if I am in error the minister can correct me. I think this is a good provision, but at the same time we must not forget our obligation to the Canadian people to see that proper testing of pesticides is carried out before they are released for general use in Canadian agriculture.

I had hoped that the department would keep matters like this in mind when drawing up the provisions for compensation. I wondered whether the department's thinking had gone that far. I realize that where it can be proved that food has been contaminated there will be compensation. because in many cases a farmer is not prepared to take action against an individual who happens to be a close friend and is the agent of a manufacturer. speechtext:
the second reading and reference to the standing committee on agriculture of Bill C-154, to prevent the introduction or spreading of pests injurious to plants.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it will take me perhaps longer than until five o'clock to give the introductory and explanatory remarks on Bill C-154.
Preventing the introduction and spread in Canada of insects and diseases destructive to our farm crops and forests is one of the most important roles performed by my department. Prevention is essential if agricultural productivity and quality are to be maintained and if expensive control and eradication programs which add greatly to cost of production are to be avoided.
The need for effective safeguards has grown as the movement of plants and plant materials in Canada and between Canada and other countries has increased. The plant protection division of my department, which administers the Destructive Insect and Pest

Act, last year issued more than 8,200 permits for importation of plants, plant materials and plant products and inspected some 282 million plants, 10,800 pounds of tree and shrub seeds, and 80,000 tons of plant products from 33 countries. There were more than 1,100 interceptions of plant parasitic insects and disease organisms, of which more than 500 were of serious nature.
The Destructive Insect and Pest Act, while it has served Canada well, was drawn up in 1910 on the premise that injurious insect pests and diseases would be excluded either by outright prohibition of host materials or by visual examination of plants and materials at the time of entry to Canada. However, the growth of international trade in agricultural products, the increasing speed of transportation and a greater knowledge of the risks involved has pointed to the necessity of introducing more modern inspection, quarantine and disinfection techniques. The new plant quarantine act, which we are proposing to replace the older legislation, provides for these newer techniques.
This bill, like its predecessor, provides authority for inspection and certification that plants and plant products being exported meet the requirements of importing countries and is essential in keeping the doors abroad open to Canadian products. Last year departmental inspectors certified for export more than six million plants, 20 million board feet of lumber, 1.4 million containers of fruit, two million hundredweight of seed potatoes, and above five million tons of cereal grains and cereal products. The standards imposed on these products by foreign countries have become increasingly stringent in recent years-a situation which makes it imperative that the department have greater authority to carry out inspection and certification programs which will ensure acceptability of Canadian products in international trade.
Prompt imposition of quarantines in affected areas is important in preventing the spread of insect pests and diseases throughout the country. One quarantine of long standing prohibits the movement from Newfoundland of certain articles and commodities capable of carrying the potato wart organism or the golden nematode. A somewhat similar quarantine was imposed on the southern part of Vancouver island following the discovery there of a golden nematode infestation in 1965. More recently, quarantine restrictions have been placed on the movement out of the province of cereal grain, hay and straw from two southwestern Ontario counties. The last
January 14, 1969

was imposed following the discovery of infestations of the cereal leaf beetle, a pest that could seriously damage cereal grain crops throughout Canada.
Although area quarantines are helpful in curbing the spread of insects and disease, there are occasions when effective control or eradication requires that individual farms be quarantined and restricted as to the kind of crops that may be grown. Such is the case with potatoes, the prime host of the golden nematode. Eradication of the nematode requires soil sterlization accompanied by a lapse in potato production for several years. But existing legislation does not provide the authority needed to restrict, from general or specific agricultural use, properties or premises which are infested or suspected of being infested. It will only take me about two minutes to finish, Mr. Speaker.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I move the second reading of Bill C-14 in a very hopeful mood. We are in the midst of a session during which all the indications are that we are going to do a lot of business. We are going to pass 40 bills in 80 days. We are moving ahead and clearing out the cobwebs and laying the groundwork for a new and more just society. This is what the papers tell us.
As a matter of fact, one of the most outspoken advocates of change is the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) who feels that the time has come for real improvements in the labour field. I think it can be said that he has already demonstrated that he means what he says. Therefore, since the bill I am presenting calls for a very modest step forward I cannot imagine that this house will do anything else but accept this motion and refer this bill to the committee in an attempt to get it on the statute books during this session of parliament.
As I say, the bill is a very simple one. It proposes that the Canada Labour (Standards) Code be amended in so far as it provides for holidays with pay. That legislation at the present time provides for two weeks holidays with pay for all employees who have at least one year's service with the same employer. The very modest proposal in Bill C-14 is that the Canada Labour (Standards) Code be amended to provide that any employee who has three years service with the same employer shall from that time on have at least three weeks annual holidays with pay each year.
I should point out that there are some collective agreements which provide even better holiday arrangements than are suggested in this bill. Likewise, there are many people in professional employment who gets this much or even more vacation in the course of a year. I am sure we all agree in principle that, with advancing technology, the need to distribute employment, and with the acceptance of the philosophy that we are here not just to work but to enjoy some of the benefits of work, it is little enough to suggest that workers in this country, certainly after three years, should enjoy at least three weeks annual holiday with pay.
I recognize that in the federal area we cannot legislate for all of the workers in this country but only for those who come under

federal labour jurisdiction, but there is a tendency in Canada for provincial labour laws to be patterned after federal labour law. I feel, therefore, that if we take this step here at the centre it will only be a matter of time until it will be the law across Canada.

maintopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE PROVISION FOR THREE WEEKS ANNUAL VACATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have read with interest some of the speeches made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey). I must say that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made an excellent choice for this very important cabinet post. The minister is a self-made man who a few years ago worked for 30 cents an hour. After long hours of hard work and study he has risen to one of the most important posts in this new government. I should like to congratulate the minister on his appointment because I believe he is the right man in the right post. Although he rose to the top he has never lost his deep concern for the working people of this nation, and he is keenly interested in all their problems.
Annual vacations with pay have been provided for by law in industry subject to federal labour jurisdiction since 1958. The first federal law, the Annual Vacations Act, required employers within its scope to grant their employees paid vacations of one week after one year of employment and two weeks after two years of service. This act was replaced in 1965 by Part III of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code which provides for a vacation with pay of at least two weeks.
I suggest that the government of this nation lead the way and take a good hard look at this bill so that employees under federal labour jurisdiction will be provided with three weeks annual vacation with pay after three years of service. I have always believed that if governments lead the way in matters concerning labour problems many labour and management disputes would disappear.

We are living in fast changing times regarding employment possibilities in this great nation. We are being forced to retrain workers as they are displaced from their jobs owing to technological change in the industries of this country. I believe that by taking a good look at this bill we could create a great many new jobs as a result of increasing employment opportunities by perhaps 2 per cent. Vacation periods could be spread over a 12 month period and we could find full time jobs for many workers. True enough, company expenses would rise a little, but on the other hand we all have to contribute through various agencies to help support people who are unable to find work.
We must all realize that not everybody in this country can attend university and become lawyers, teachers, doctors, dentists, engineers and so on. Somewhere along the line people have to do the work in industries and it is up to us in this house to provide the necessary jobs so that men can provide their wives and families with the necessities of life and live with dignity.
Industries across this nation have in the past tried to be good members of our society, but sometimes they are slow to change with the times. I think it is time that the legislators of this nation established the best minimum standards and working conditions, and let collective bargaining take over from there.
The proposed standard in Bill C-14 of three weeks vacation after three years of employment with the same employer is still somewhat in advance of present practice in industry generally, although in the past three years there has been a trend toward this standard upon completion of a lesser number of years of service. The 1965 working conditions survey reported in the Canada Department of Labour publication "Labour Conditions in Canadian Industry, 1965" showed that for all non-office employees surveyed, approximately two million or 27 per cent received three weeks annual vacation after less than ten years service. The same survey showed that for all office employees surveyed, approximately 950,000, 46 per cent, received three weeks annual vacation after less than three years service.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The 1967 survey shows that for all nonoffice employees surveyed, two and a quarter million, 38 per cent, received three weeks vacation, 12 per cent of them after less than five years service. The same survey shows
January 14, 1969

that for all office employees surveyed, 1,100,000, 53 per cent, received three weeks vacation, 22 per cent of them after less than five years service. A further 51 per cent of nonoffice employees received three weeks vacation after periods of 10 to 15 years service, and 1 per cent received three weeks vacation after 15 years of service. In the case of office employees, 36 per cent received three weeks vacation after periods of 10 to 15 years of service, and 1 per cent after 15 years of service.
I believe these figures show that we are moving in the direction of three weeks vacation for all workers. I also believe that in our society we must change our thinking and that the time is ripe for making an advance with this kind of legislation. We ought to ensure that there are good minimum vacation standards for people in the labouring field, who need holidays more than any others. All people, whether members of this house or not, are aware that there are today increasing pressures on family life. It is also true to say that in most cases members of families do not know each other well; they do not enjoy the day to day contact which is needed for a strong family life.
We live in a society that is travelling so fast that both parents have to go to work daily in order to pay for the necessities of life. The only time the family can enjoy themselves as a family group is on Sunday and during the family vacation. It may not be possible to take action this afternoon in this regard, but I do hope this bill will be given serious consideration by parliament because as the affluent society becomes more and more productive it is our desire that it will no longer be necessary for people to continue to work as hard as they have in the past.

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to take part in the same debate with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) this afternoon. He is one of the most senior members in this house and his sincere concern for social justice is well known. Nineteen years ago, while in my last year of the modern history course at the University of Toronto, I wrote an essay for my professor, Mr. Frank Underhill, on James S. Woodsworth, the first leader of the C.C.F. party who held the seat of Winnipeg North Centre continuously from 1921 until his death in 1942. The present member for Winnipeg North Centre, who was elected to the seat on Mr. Woodsworth's death, had been a member of this house for seven years when I wrote that essay, and at that time I certainly had no idea that I would be debating with him in the House of Commons nearly 20 years later.

January 14. 1969
Vacation Leave Bill
While checking into the background of Bill C-14 it was very interesting to read the debates in Hansard on similar bills that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre introduced in recent years. In August, 1964, the hon. member moved second reading of a bill to provide for three weeks vacation with pay to all those workers in Canada under federal jurisdiction, including railway, transportation and communication workers, bank employees, etc., as long as they had been employed by the same employer for five years.
The relevant federal legislation at that time provided for one week's vacation after one year's employment and for two weeks vacation after two years employment. The government speakers in that debate stated, among other things, that since a comprehensive labour code was going to be introduced by the Liberal government in the near future, amendments of this kind should not be made piece by piece in the meantime.
In 1965 the Canada Labour (Standards) Code was passed by parliament, which among other things provided for two weeks annual vacation with pay for all workers under federal jurisdiction who had worked for the same employer for one year. Then in March, 1967, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre moved second reading of a bill similar to the one now before us, calling for three weeks vacation after working for three years for the same employer. In October, 1967, a similar bill was again brought forward by the hon. member.
While only about one-tenth of the labour force in Canada comes under federal jurisdiction and the remaining 90 per cent under provincial jurisdiction, all labour legislation passed in Ottawa is important, not only because of its direct effect on the 10 per cent under federal jurisdiction but also because it should show the way for the provinces and give them the incentive to provide better minimum labour legislation for the 90 per cent of employees directly under their jurisdiction.
I believe the federal government should definitely lead the way in reform labour legislation, as in reform legislation of all kinds. However, since such federal labour legislation tends to be so influential on similar provincial legislation, the federal legislation has to be well considered and realistic because of its effect on the whole economy of our country.

[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
As has been pointed out, only one province, Saskatchewan, requires three weeks paid holidays, and that after five years of employment, while four provinces require two weeks holidays, four provinces require one week's holidays, and one has no legislation dealing with annual vacations at all.
In the 1967 survey prepared by the Canadian Department of Labour only 12 per cent of non-office employees and 22 per cent of office employees in all industries received three weeks vacation with pay after working less than five years. The same 1967 survey shows that in industries under federal jurisdiction only 5.1 per cent of non-office employees and 6.6 per cent of office employees received three weeks vacation after working less than five years. Accordingly, an amendment to our Canada Labour (Standards) Code making three weeks vacation compulsory after only three years service would be too sudden an economic change, not only for the industries under federal jurisdiction but also too sudden for the provinces to implement in the near future for the industries under their jurisdiction.
I am sure everyone in the house is generally in favour of longer and longer vacations with pay, and with the rapid increase of automation and the resulting increased productivity of each worker there is no doubt that paid vacation periods will become longer and longer. I hope and expect that federal labour legislation will be in the forefront in promoting this. I do not wish to be harsh but while the general intent of the hon. member's bill is commendable, it shows the lack of practicality and responsibility which members of his party often portray, because they know that they will never have to assume the reins of government and so will never have to try to carry out any of their proposed legislation. It would have been just as easy and had as much practical effect if the hon. member had proposed three weeks holidays after two years service or three weeks holidays after one year's service since the hon. member knows that he will never have to take the responsibility for any such legislation as a member of a government party.
In addition to two weeks paid vacation after one year of service the Canada Labour (Standards) Code also insists on eight legal holidays with pay as a minimum requirement for industries under federal jurisdiction. The provisions in the Canada Labour (Standards) Code are, of course minimum provisions and
January 14, 1S69

Vacation Leave Bill
there is nothing to prevent the negotiation of longer paid holidays by collective bargaining between union and management or between an individual employee and employer in cases where there is not a union.
A great number of collective bargaining agreements provide for three weeks and longer vacation periods, but very few have obtained them for three years employment or less. I suspect the reason for this is that the unions themselves do not generally believe it is reasonable to ask for three weeks vacation after only three years of employment, and so they press for matters which they feel will be considered more reasonable, namely, increased wages, better working conditions, more attractive pension plans, etc.
In the debate on a similar bill in March 1967, referred to previously, the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) who represented the former riding of Prince at that time, spoke quite clearly on the need for longer vacations because of the ever-increasing pressures of modern life on the family unit. However, he went on to discuss the problems of longer periods of leisure for most people who have not learned to use their leisure creatively.
I certainly hope and expect that we will be able to keep increasing the minimum length of paid vacations by amending existing federal labour legislation from time to time and that in the meantime the federal government and all levels of government will encourage and actively support various types of programs that will enable people of all ages to learn to use their leisure time more happily and effectively.
In conclusion I would like to say that a three week annual vacation with pay for a relatively short term of employment is on the horizon and will be commonly accepted within a few years. However, for present economic reasons the bill before us this afternoon is a little premature.

maintopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE PROVISION FOR THREE WEEKS ANNUAL VACATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for his Bill C-14. It seems to me that the federal labour code is continually being shortcircuited by collective bargaining and by labour unions negotiating the basis of contracts and fringe benefits in various parts of the country, and that we have found it less necessary to amend the labour code in order to provide definite guidelines or laws with respect to the length of vacations that we think our people should have. On the one
hand we co-operate with the labour unions through our manpower and labour departments. We try to work in co-operation with them so that they can institute collective bargaining and handle the vacation and pay aspects. On the other hand it is being suggested that we should establish just what these should be by providing three weeks vacation after three years of service.
I presume it would be somewhat dangerous for me to say that employees should not have three weeks vacation, and I will not say it. However, I am concerned about vacations which become periods of moonlighting. While I agree with my good friend, the hon. member for London East (Mr. Turner), I must say that if people definitely went on vacations I believe it would be of great assistance to the Canadian economy. One of the problems I have noticed over the years, especially in recent years when people have had so much spare time anyway, unless they happen to be members of parliament, is that a great deal of moonlighting is taking place in people's spare time. This creates a problem.
It is my belief that we should endeavour to increase productivity so as to reduce the inflation which is confronting us at present and in this way earn a three weeks vacation which can then be taken and enjoyed. I firmly believe, as does the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that people are entitled to this holiday and should have it. I may say that I am a little confused by the proposed section 16 which reads in part as follows:
-provided however that every employee who has had three years of continuous employment by one employer is entitled to and shall be granted a vacation with vacation pay of at least three weeks.
I wonder if this could be explained for my benefit because it seems to me it should read: "shall be granted a vacation with pay or vacation pay of at least three weeks." In other words, I do not believe it is required in the labour code that if a person received a vacation he should also receive vacation pay. In this case it would have to be 6 per cent, as I understand it, over and above the regular pay he would get when taking a vacation.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
There is a great deal of work to be done in Canada in cementing relations between labour and management. Labour organizations must accept responsibility as soon as possible for taking a fearless look at the problem of productivity. At the same time, they must receive our support in seeing to it that

January 14. 1969
Vacation Leave Bill
people who work a given number of hours receive the vacation that is due them; that productivity in Canada is stepped up; and that we are all able to enjoy a much rosier economic picture than is in view at this time.

maintopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE PROVISION FOR THREE WEEKS ANNUAL VACATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the most qualified people to speak on the advantages of a three-week vacation are the members of this house who have just enjoyed one. Indeed, they might add to what has already been said about the advantage of having three weeks instead of two, because if we had only two weeks we would have returned here a week ago. I think we might also relate the question of holidays to the question of productivity. I am not so sure that in embarking upon this type of analysis I would agree with the conclusion expressed by the previous speaker.
This subject is certainly one which has engaged the attention of people throughout the world. Perhaps hon. members might be interested in a few remarks which were made 14 years ago in Geneva on the occasion of the 37th session of the International Labour Conference by one of the delegates who gave a brief analysis of what, in his opinion, an annual paid holiday meant. He said:
There is no doubt that annual paid holidays have biological, social and economic objectives. First, they enable the worker to recuperate psychologically and physiologically, after his hard year's work. Secondly, holidays enable him to change his surroundings and engage in cultural recreation, sport or travel; this is socially useful as well as providing a solution for the fatigue problem, for rest without change is not sufficient for him to recover his strength and his ability to do his job. This brings me to the economic objective, for the holiday enables the worker to recover his productive power.
However, scientific experiments have shown that in order to achieve these objects it is necessary that the holiday should not be less than two weeks, for if it is shorter the worker will return to his employment without having recovered his biological balance.
On that occasion the convention endorsed and ratified the principle of two weeks' holiday after one year of employment. As I say, this was 14 years ago at a time when automation was perhaps just beginning to make itself felt.
The bill as placed before the house by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is one which perhaps deserves thorough analysis, if only for the reason that a 50 year old employee who because of automation and dislocation in industry has to change his employment from one company to another under federal jurisdiction would find himself

starting again at the bottom of the ladder, thus receiving shorter holidays than an employee aged 23 who commenced employment three years before at the age of 20. Such a man at age 50 would perhaps require three weeks' holiday far more than his junior colleague.
We are living in a time of automation which requires dislocation of employment. Therefore rigid approaches to questions of holidays may not be entirely suitable. It seems to me that while the federal government has to set the pace in certain broad areas, and will do so, at the same time it has to approach the matter in a flexible manner, perhaps reflecting in its deliberations and final decisions a concept of holidays that is related to the age of the worker.
We all know that a worker at the advanced age of 60 might require a longer holiday than a worker aged 25 or 30. Therefore I think the whole question requires study. Rather than boxing it in within the scheme proposed, we should study the question of dislocation caused by automation and the development of human resources. We might perhaps ask the question: Why only three weeks after three years? It might well be the case that a longer holiday is required in certain segments of industry that warrant it and a shorter holiday in others that do not. As some hon. members have already indicated, there has to be a certain relationship between holidays and productivity.
I agree we must recognize the fact that the federal government sets the pace for the private sector, and an initiative of this kind would have this effect. But rather than go into the question in this manner it seems to me we should approach it in greater depth, and before making a final decision analyse all of the factors that I have briefly outlined.

maintopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE PROVISION FOR THREE WEEKS ANNUAL VACATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I shall give my opinion on the bill brought forward by the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
It is obvious at once that this bill will meet the approval of all legislators, who must necessarily be interested in the Canadian workers' lot.
In view of the constantly increasing pace at which our society is evolving, we know that owing to the progress of technology, the number of working hours is bound to decrease, and that consequently within a few years, we shall have to give serious consideration to
January 14, 1969

organizing the leisure of the Canadian people, who, may be, will want to specialize in the field of research, in order to further develop our country and the rest of the world.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Of course, the purpose of the bill is readily understood, since the title is as follows:
An Act to amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code (Three Weeks Annual Vacation after Three Years).
Theoretically, this is a very good thing, but a hasty application of this measure would probably result in numerous complications.
At present, under the Canada Labour Code, if I am not mistaken an employer is required to grant an employee two weeks vacation with pay after a year of employment.
I think it is necessary to add, and I emphasize the fact, that eight days of vacation with pay, eight statutory holidays, are granted anyway according to the Labour Code, over those two weeks vacation.
The honourable member for Winnipeg North Centre, as I said earlier-if my memory serves me right-always shows a great deal of perseverance and consistency in his views. I think that we can congratulate him for this positive approach which he has always cultivated and which can be rated among his good intellectual habits.
In fact, we can notice that the sponsor of this bill already introduced a similar bill in April 1965. He also introduced one in 1964 when he suggested that a three weeks annual vacation with pay should be granted to an employee after five years of employment with the same employer and I notice that, at the outset of the debate, the honourable member for Halifax recalled the basic principles which had been used when preparing the Canada Labour Code.
The code was based on the principle whereby it was important to set up minimum standards because it could be dangerous for the balance of our industry to aim towards standards setting up too high maximums. In order to adopt such measures, in spite of the good intentions of those who wished to introduce them, we are still convinced that several years of research or experience are necessary.
I have opposed the opinion formerly expressed by the member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) when he said that by implementing such a measure overnight once again the consumer would foot the bill, once again mothers and small wage earners would suffer heavy
Vacation Leave Bill
deprivations. The honourable member mentioned also the financial difficulties the adoption of this act could mean for small Canadian industrialists and businessmen.
The standards proposed by the bill stipulate a three-week holiday after three years of employment. Those standards outdistance by far present practice in industry, not only that which falls within federal jurisdiction, but industry in general. Looking at working conditions in the Canadian industry in 1964, as reported in a publication of the Department of Labour, and in the industries that fall within federal jurisdiction, we note that this practice is far from a minimum and far from general. Instead of generalizing it, a study should be made of the evolution through the years.
We then see that only 12 per cent of the employees, other than office personnel, have three weeks off after less than 10 years of employment. Of all employees, office and others,-of which there were 2,500,000-15 per cent only had a three-week holiday after less than 10 years of service. Granting three weeks of holidays after relatively short periods of service was far more general amongst office personnel, perhaps because of the more sedentary nature of the work. Numerous other statistics could show us how complicated it would be to apply this legislative measure immediately. Looking at figures, for instance, in the article "Vacations with pay 1964, all industries", we note that:
s (5:50 p.m.)

Total number of reporting units, non office employees, 19,057. Office employees, 19,267.

The number of those who enjoy a three weeks annual vacation with pay, after less than ten years of service, amounts to 15 per cent while for the office workers, the proportion is only of 26 per cent. After ten years of employment, for the non-office employees, the proportion is 22 per cent compared with 26 per cent for the office employees.
It is clear that for most businesses which give three weeks annual vacation or more to employees with several years of service, the length of service is much more than three years.
It would be advisable also, I think, after a study of what happens in practice with regard to vacation in the industry and businesses in general, to study the policy followed by the provinces.

January 14, 1966
Vacation Leave Bill
In Saskatchewan, for example, according to the Labour Code, employees can enjoy two weeks annual vacation after one year, and three weeks after five years.
Three other provinces, Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia, legislated so that the employee would have two weeks annual vacation after one year of service.
Four provinces, Nova Scotia, Quebec, Ontario and New Brunswick, legislated so that the employee would only get one week vacation.
Two provinces, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island, have passed no legislation on this subject up to now, at least as far as I know.
With regard to the Canada Labour Code, we know that the labour standards came into force on July 1, 1965. With this code, the vacation period extended from one week to two weeks for employees with one year of service, taking into consideration the eight general statutory holidays

the eight non working days-with pay, as I mentioned earlier. That was, a few years ago, a substantial improvement in the case of numerous employees.
A proposal such as the one in the bill now under study, that would increase substantially the standards concerning annual vacations, could hardly be seriously considered at this time. I think it would also be wise to consider the International Labour Organization in this field.
According to the 1964 statistics, a group of experts has already completed the study of that problem throughout the world and come to the conclusion that there was a tendency to extend the vacation period in numerous industries.
As regards the future, one would obviously hope to grant three weeks annual vacation, but not at this time, because of the complexities involved and of the general practice.
It is, at present, the best solution. Such was my opinion in the past as it still is now. I believe it is in accordance with the principles of our party and with the respect due to private enterprise.
When I think of private enterprise, I do not think only of the boss or the owner but of the employees also. That is why I find it normal, since a reasonable minimum is already provided in our Labour Code, to leave to collective bargaining the task of setting the length of the annual holidays in relation to the years of service and of discussing the matter with the bosses taking into account the nature of

the industry, the work, the number of employees and a host of other conditions we all know. We must all ask ourselves how far the legislators should go when setting minimum standards for working conditions, without interfering in the field of collective bargaining, and I think that it is one of the basic principles which inspired the people who drafted our Labour Code-and who are still working on it

to improve our labour legislation and the lot of the Canadian workers.
Where the labour market is steady enough to enable an employee to accumulate several years of continuous employment for the same employer, it seems that there is no obstacle to an effective trade union organization. The present government, just like those preceding it, has taken a great interest in the improvement of labour conditions. In fact, we know that the question of holidays, of annual vacations, holds more and more the attention and to what extent the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEaehen) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) concern themselves in retraining our labour force, in order to enable it to play an effective part in our country.
Our Speeches from the Throne, which always reflect the principles of our governments, have never neglected the labour policy, as shown by the legislation passed during the last session and by the bills now appearing on the order paper. It is obvious that in all areas of Canada, we must have healthy workers and that we must take their needs into account by granting them reasonable holidays. But the government which is responsibly playing its part cannot infringe on the rights and privileges of the Canadian people. This is why we are always striving in that field to provide maximum justice.

Mr. Speaker, in making my remarks on this bill I shall endeavour to be very brief. Sometimes the extent of the repercussions of this playing around have been somewhat painful. When mankind has tried to introduce various and sundry plant, animal and insect life into his environment in the hope it would help him, even if the help is only of an aesthetic nature, sometimes the long term effect has been, if not harmful to health, at least a pain in the neck.
One can think of examples such as the sparrow, the starling and the Colorado beetle which are hardly native to Canada. Then, there is the spruce budworm and the Dutch elm disease which we still cannot learn how to control now that they are here. I do not envy the Minister of Agriculture and his officials who will have to make very great efforts in order to bring this type of thing under control. In Saskatchewan a story is told about a person who claimed an exemption on his income tax. He said a horsefly got in with the bees and all the honey tasted like horse manure, so he could not sell it.
In respect of the import and export of what this bill calls pests I might say that I always considered these insects to be Liberals, but the bill gives a much broader definition. done with regard to the supervision and control of the import and export of these commodities, there is a need for further control. speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COMPENSATION APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
second reading and reference to the standing committee on agriculture of Bill C-156, to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the proposed amendments to the Animal Contagious Diseases Act embody two major changes. One deals with the way in which compensation rates are set for animals ordered slaughtered. The second provides for an appeal by the owner against a compensation award under the act.
For the past 43 years the federal government has compensated owners of animals that have been ordered destroyed under eradication programs for Johne's disease, brucellosis and tuberculosis.
Up to now, compensation rates have been prescribed in the act. From 1925 to 1949 the compensation rates were a maximum of $60 for grade cattle and $150 for purebred cattle. The basis for this compensation was two-thirds of the value of the animals slaughtered.
January 14, 1989	COMMONS
In 1949, the compensation rates were revised to provide a maximum of $40 for grade cattle and $100 for purebred cattle. The full value was paid up to the maximum rate. In the last revision in 1968, rates were established at a maximum of $70 for grade and $140 for purebred.
The owner's total return for an animal ordered slaughtered is the meat salvage value plus the compensation awarded by the government. Where the sale of the animal's carcass is unlawful an additional amount equal to the value the carcass would have had if the sale were lawful is paid by the government.
The proposed revision retains this provision so that the farmer would either be able to recover the meat salvage value by selling the carcass or, where this is forbidden, by recovering the carcass value from the government. The amendment provided is that compensation rates would no longer be set by the act. These maximum rates would be established by the governor in council. This would allow a more flexible approach to compensation. Value of purebred livestock and, indeed, of grade dairy cattle for instance, can change markedly even within a year's time.
The second change being proposed is the amendment to provide for appeal against a compensation award. At the present time no such appeal is available. The amended act would permit the owner of an animal ordered slaughtered to appeal against the amount of the award or to appeal where no compensation is awarded at all under the appeal provisions included in the pesticide residue compensation act. The appeal privilege would not delay the destruction of diseased animals.
This bill, C-156 relates directly to some of the provisions of Bill C-155. I am not going to go over them, but the procedures there are the same. Bill No. C-156 cites Bill C-155 and its provisions as the procedure used when an appeal against compensation is being made by the farmer.

In the past farmers have been paid at a very low rate for animals which have been destroyed once they were contaminated by a contagious disease. This has caused great hardship. In some cases, for instance in respect of dairy herds, this has driven particular farmers into bankruptcy. We think this bill will give the individual farmers much more

Animal Contagious Diseases Act insurance. We are also very happy to note that the farmer will have the right to appeal against the judgment of a particular assessor.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
In this light we think the bill certainly has merit and we go along with it in every respect. I know it is very closely related to the bills we have been discussing today and we believe it is a step in the right direction in the field of agriculture. I note there are some other fields that are not covered by the bill. At other stages of the bill these matters can be given consideration. I am sure that farmers in some other fields are subjected to loss because of contagious diseases contracted by their herds and I think it is only fair that they should be compensated. They have been compensated to a degree but the farmers themselves have had to undergo long and very painful treatment.
