subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COMPENSATION APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for a long time the matter of changing the compensation in respect of animal contagious diseases has been under consideration by a committee of the house; in fact, ever since I have been here. I presume there are few members in the house who remember the problem that developed in respect of scabies in sheep and the political repercussions of the Gardiner days with regard to that problem. Therefore I ask, why has September 26 been chosen as the cut-off date? Has it any significance? I presume the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) expected us to pass this measure long before now, and that is the significance.
The matter of compensation is a unique one in terms of animals that are slaughtered, in that the nation's agricultural community is always concerned when there is an outbreak of a contagious disease. I can remember back to those days when there were throughout the
January 14, 1969

Animal Contagious Diseases Act country dozens and dozens of herds that suffered contagious abortion. These herds were kept and milked. There was nothing wrong with maintaining a brucellosis herd. These cows continued to give milk and were part of an economic unit.
I am not suggesting that we go back to those days, because I think Canada should be very proud of the job that has been done by the Canadian veterinarian service in the eradication of this and almost every other contagious disease in the animal field. The job that has been done with regard to brucellosis control has meant that most of the farming areas in Canada are brucellosis free. The eradication of this disease has been brought about over a period of time and, with a great deal of education, has been highly successful.
Therefore there will not be many cases of brucellosis. There will not be many epidemics of t.b., scabies or any of the other diseases faced in the agricultural field. There are three diseases that we, hopefully, will not have to face in epidemic proportions. One is foot and mouth disease, which of course is in a totally different category from the other diseases about which we have been speaking because in the case of the contagious diseases of scabies, brucellosis and t.b. it is not likely that they will again reach epidemic proportions.
We go into an area and ask a farmer to allow the government to control his herd until the disease is eradicated. We will be doing this not only to the advantage of the farmer but in a wider sense to the advantage of the community and the whole area. This is very true in respect of brucellosis control. For this reason, I do not think we should be so niggardly about the compensation that we pay. If a person has a good herd, the compensation that will be paid by order in council will probably not be much more satisfactory than that paid under the present regulations.
If a farmer has a low grade herd which has contracted brucellosis, the meat can be used and if meat prices are reasonably high he will, with the compensation, probably realize the value of the animal. I suppose it is very difficult to talk about an average in this regard, but I presume that the average, registered dairy cow today is worth approximately $700 to $800. Some of them run as high as $40,000, and I suppose they go down to $250. But the average would, I think, be well over $700. Why, then, should we ask the farmer to bear the whole brunt of the brucellosis control in his area when he may not have had anything to do with the introduction


of brucellosis? Therefore I suggest we should be much more generous in this field and make payment on the basis of fair sale value. If the cow is worth $700 we should make up the total value of the animal, taking into consideration the sale of the meat. We should make a settlement on the basis of the total value of the animal. This is not very much. Last year we paid out a very small amount of money in respect of this control.
However, one of these days, unfortunate as it may be, we will again have an epidemic of one of these animal diseases. We are no more immune to an outbreak of anthrax or foot and mouth disease than other countries which established these kind of controls a long time ago. There is no reason why a farmer would try to cover up the disease for a period of time because everyone in the agricultural community realizes that it must be taken care of at the earliest possible date.
We saw last year in England the eradication of a large percentage of the agricultural production in certain sections of the dairy industry. Canada should be proud of the assistance given by the Canadian veterinarian department which went to their aid on that occasion. But this was a calamity; it was a major emergency. I would like to see the retention of any control under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act that will work toward the immediate eradication of a disease that is contracted by a herd. The regulations that will be passed will not be in that field. If they are, let us make them the regulations and let us say so. This raises another problem. There might be another outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease at which time a farmer may lose his whole herd through no fault of

Mr. Speaker,
I have the honour to represent a mixed territory, that is a territory where industry and
farming live side by side, and as far as cattle breeding is concerned, there are many model farmers in my region because they do everything they can to improve their herds as much as possible.
One knows, for instance, that over the last ten years many of those farmers took advantage of the services provided by the artificial insemination centre in Saint-Hyacinthe and for 50 years those cattle breeders have been choosing their breeding stock with the utmost care. They never hesitated either to make rather important purchases of better developed choice animals when the results expected from their cattle were too long in coming.
Finally, I can say that during that period those farmers benefitted to a great extent from the advantages put at their disposal by the provincial and federal governments, such as the grants for the purchase of good cattle as well as the advice about feeding and other matters given by the government technicians. It goes without saying that such an improvement does not come about without the cattle breeders spending large sums of money, since the operation costs of a farm have been increasing from year to year.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, at first sight Bill No. C-156 now before the house could make us happy because it proposes amendments to increase the compensation to be paid for animals to be destroyed because of contagious diseases. In fact, experience has taught me that the present compensation was not very fair in view of the economic changes the farmers must take into account, and the amount of $70 for destroying grade animals, as well as the amount of $140 for pure bred animals, which was set in 1958, is clearly not enough if one considers that a Holstein cow values between $175 and $200 ten years ago is now worth between $450 and $600. I will not go as far as to insist on the figures quoted by the previous speaker who mentioned a cow worth $40,000, because there are only one or two in a constituency. At any rate, we have generally referred to cattle worth $500 to $600


and for all those reasons an amendment to the legislation is essential.
However, the main object of the bill is to withdraw the amounts paid as compensations and the following recommendations can be read:
His Excellency the governor general has recommended to the house the present measure to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act to remove from the act the amounts of compensation specified for the horses and cattle slaughtered pursuant to the act and to permit the governor in council to prescribe maximum amounts for such compensation;
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that bill will give rise to patronage and I quote paragraph (b) of section 1:
-such value to be determined by the minister or by some person appointed by him for that purpose.
Mr. Speaker, there is no problem, because as stated by a Montreal commentator, the minister is well-informed about cows since he owns 250. At the present time, the minister is assisted by technicians-former members of the Cooperative federee and farmers-and I feel that it is no longer necessary to worry about the bill now under consideration. But let us suppose that one day or another a minister is inexperienced-it has happened, Mr. Speaker, because he may be a lawyer or an economist, in short, a person who has never seen a cow and could barely tell a dog from a cat-he could refer to another provision of the legislation, because in fact, it has been specifically expected that mistakes could be made and I quote:
-to provide also for an appeal by the owners of animals slaughtered where no compensation or less compensation than the maximum prescribed is awarded to the owners.
Mr. Speaker, in such a case, if the minister is not sufficiently informed, he would be compelled to appoint someone who would be in a position to apply the act adequately. However, if the person who has been elected is a Liberal condidate who, for instance, was defeated in the last election, and goes in a riding to assess the herd of a Conservative, of a Creditiste or a political organizer, one can imagine what kind of assessment this will be. In a case like this, the farmer will have to appeal again to the board. I am quoting section 2, which says that an ordinary civil servant is to assess the value:
-where no compensation is awarded for that animal on the ground that the failure to award compensation was unreasonable.

One can easily imagine how easily a farmer will be sent packing. I am quoting further:
Every appeal to the assessor referred to in subsection (1) shall be brought within three months from the date the owner receives notification of the decision or the compensation that is the subject of the appeal or within such longer period as the assessor may in any case for special reasons allow.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat that this is just political manoevring, which will only result in arousing discontent and creating problems which will have to be solved by other civil servants.
I submit we have enough civil servants as it is. Are we going to hire some more people to correct mistakes? Though it is rather complicated, but it is a way of hiding the unemployment situation.
The fact that the rate of compensation was changed only twice in 20 years proves that we have allowed ourselves to be outdistanced in that field. Standards must be set ahead of time to ensure compensation that is proportionate to the losses incurred. To my mind, those standards are also necessary to give renewed confidence to the stock-breeder and keep him from delays in revealing cases of illness in his herd because, as you are aware, when illness strikes a herd, for lack of capital, a farmer could refrain from reporting the facts and so be responsible for the resulting epidemic.
For all those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I feel that this should be looked into seriously. I bring my remarks to a close by saying again to the hon. minister that I am convinced of the danger inherent in leaving it to one or two civil servants to set the amount of compensation. I ask him to tell us what he intends to do to improve this bill which must have been drawn up by some incompetent person. However, as I know he is acquainted with the problem, I should like him to reassure us and tell us what he intends to do to correct the situation.

subtopic: REGULATION OF PRODUCTS USED IN CONTROL PROCEDURE

speechtext:
Hon. H. A, Olson (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading and reference to the standing committee on agriculture of bill C-157, to regulate products used for the control of pests and the organic functions of plants and animals.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the last of the four bills that, as I said earlier this afternoon, are related. Hon. gentlemen will realize, of course, that pesticides have a great deal to do with the high standard of living enjoyed by
January 14, 1369

the average Canadian today. Not only do they enable farmers to produce greater quantities of high quality food more economically, but they also make it possible for all of us to live, work, and play in considerable more comfort than did our forefathers.
The list of pests arrayed against us is formidable. There are about 2,500 different kinds of insects and related organisms that from time to time attack Canadian crops and gardens. There are 2,000 plant diseases. There are 1,000 kinds of weeds. There are several hundred kinds of animal diseases and other animal pests to plague us.
It is estimated that one third of all crops is lost to weeds, pests, and disease. What would be the toll without pesticides? It is a fact that some crops just could not be grown at all without chemical help, while the yields of other crops would be greatly reduced. Food quality would also suffer because many items would be infected with worms, fungi and insects.
The agricultural community is naturally the big consumer of pesticides but these chemicals also have hundreds of uses in industry and in the home. Fumigants kill bugs in warehouses; growth suppressants keep down weeds on airports; insecticides kill aphids on ornamental trees; rodenticides rid our houses of mice; repellants keep dogs away from flowers, and so on. There is a very long list of these chemicals that are useful.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
I think hon. members will also realize that pesticides are opening up new recreational areas, allowing us to use what were previously unbearable locations. Pesticides are now a very important part of all our lives. We certainly could not live in the style to which we have become accustomed without them. But pesticides have dual personalities. It is true that they bring us untold benefits, but they can also get us into trouble if they are not handled properly. Careless use of pesticides can lead to food contamination, damage to crops, as well as human and animal injury.
I have mentioned that scientists are making steady progress in coming up with new and alternative methods of controlling pests, such as improved management practices, resistant crops and biological control. But these alternate controls are not yet adequate to protect crops, gardens, animals, or indeed ourselves, and therefore pesticides will be needed far into the foreseeable future.
Government control of the manufacture and use of these potentially dangerous substances is necessary if we are to protect peo-
Control of Plant Pests
pie from the misuse of pesticides. My department registered more than 3,300 different pesticides for use in Canada during the past year. This great number indicates something of the difficulty of the job of keeping tab on ail these different pest control products. To do this job adequately we need the very best, most modern legislation possible.
The bill now before us, in general terms, brings the Pest Control Products Act of 1939 up to date. While it is framed in the same general context there are some significant differences and improvements. The increased use of pesticides and associated products, and a greater concern over their potential for harm as well as good necessitate a broader authority for regulation than in the past. This is provided in the proposed legislation by adding the authority to regulate the manufacture, handling, use and advertising of such control products. Authority is also included to regulate manufacturing establishments in regard to prescribed control products for export or interprovincial movement. The present act provides only for the regulation of the product itself as to composition, packaging and labelling.
In addition to true pesticides, the new legislation also applies to other control products and products to be used along with or as a supplement to pesticides and control products. The present act provides only for the regulation of actual pest control products. Examples of products covered by the proposed legislation, not covered under the present act, would be plant growth modifiers such as sprout inhibitors, potato top killers, and fruit stop-drop sprays; emulsifiers, stickers and stabilizers for use with pesticides and other control products.
We have also provided for protection against the danger of cross contamination. For example, cross contamination could occur when the same mixing equipment is used for different pesticides. Two chemicals might be perfectly harmless by themselves but when mixed they are sometimes lethal. Cross contamination could also occur when control products are stored near food, and the use of a pesticide on food crops at harvest time could cause residues that are harmful.
The present act does provide some protection for the public against deception in merchandizing pesticides but only indirectly. This bill permits more specific control over certain labelling, advertising, and packaging practices that are difficult to regulate at present. For example, the use of numbers in the

January 14. 1969
Control of Plant Pests
brand name of products may bear no relation to the strength of a product even though it could be construed as doing so. Potentially hazardous compounds may be packaged in containers that resemble other harmless commodities. The new legislation retains the authority of the present act to regulate products through registration, standards and labelling, but adds authority over packaging.
Authority is provided in the bill for registration of premises in which certain prescribed control products may be manufactured for subsequent shipment interprovincially or abroad. These prescribed products could include those which include living organisms in their manufacture. These organisms could pose a public hazard if not handled properly. Indications are that this type of control product will be in production soon and special regulatory powers will be necessary to ensure effectiveness and safety.
In my view, this new legislation will continue to give effective service to the agricultural industry while at the same time providing greatly improved means of protecting the public interest. In conclusion, I should say that the cost of administration will increase somewhat as regulations are approved covering the new activities, and we estimate that the total additional costs would be approximately $60,000 annually when the regulations are fully implemented.

subtopic: REGULATION OF PRODUCTS USED IN CONTROL PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a prelude to my remarks in respect of Bill C-157, I would like to make these observations. The life of the pioneers of this continent was hard but simple. They were farmers and hunters living in isolation in small communities, unconcerned about the outside world. Their existence was free of many of the problems facing the people of this the twentieth century which, in many instances, have been created by the exploitation of succeeding generations. It has been stated that two grim spectres beckon mankind toward oblivion. One offers instant wholesale death by nuclear means and the other guarantees eventual starvation when the population exceeds the food supply. The powers that be in our world of today are struggling in an all out effort to postpone these evil days.
I propose to deal with this bill only in respect of how its aspects affect our food. Man is rapidly changing those once immutable features around him, the soil, atmosphere and water, even our seas and their complete production. The basic conflict is between the mounting need for food and fibre and the

equally urgent need to preserve the quality of our environment. This is the perspective in which to view the continuing debate over the value and hazards of pesticides and drugs. I mention drugs because they do relate to certain organic functions in animals.
Of course, the use of pesticides and drugs is not the only way in which man is unrespectful of his environment. The growth of cities, clearing of forests or draining of swamps, the future prospect of weather control, run away population, the adulteration of foods-all of these promise to change this once undisturbed earth irrevocably. Men can no longer approach nature merely to exploit her. They must now learn to manage her wisely. They must decide what kind of environment they really want, what quality of life they desire.
If we talk of pesticides and drugs only in terms of benefits and hazards, we fail to grapple with the basic question. Men do need to know exactly what these chemicals do and what liabilities their use may incur. But then we must decide whether, where, and how to use them to help build the kind of world we want. This is where Bill C-157 can play a very important part.
To my knowledge, the pesticides most widely used are D.D.T. and its breakdown products, aldrin, dieldrin and lindane. In experiments and studies reported to have been carried out by specialists of the University of Miami School of Medicine concentrations of D.D.T. and dieldrin were found in many humans. Traces of pesticides were found in the tissues of stillborn and unborn babies. The greatest concentrations were found in the fat tissue, but the liver, kidney and brain also carried the residue.
At this time I would like to put on the record an excerpt from an article that appeared in the Globe and Mail a few months ago under the heading, "Pesticides Held Threat to Unborn." It reads:
"An expectant mother can poison her unborn child by drinking milk from a cow that has browsed on forage sprayed by some insecticides," an official of the National Health and Welfare Department said not long ago when addressing 75 pilots attending an aerial pest control conference sponsored by the Ontario health department.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
It was further stated that careless crop spraying can have far-reaching effects. Chlorinated hydro-carbons used in some pesticides have the longest effects and can be stored in fat deposits and in milk in cattle.
January 14, 1963

One authority said that insecticides coupled with the effect of radio-active fall out could produce babies with two heads and six fingers. A survey of short horn cows found a ratio of 30 parts of insecticide to one million parts of milk. An infant child does not have the resistance to insecticides that an adult has and therefore is vulnerable.
It seems also that it would be difficult to deny the use of pesticides has caused death in fish and seagull populations. D.D.T. deposits have been found in fish. This situation is of concern to government wild life and fisheries departments. It is now evident that with the indiscriminate use of insecticides there is a danger that man eventually will not be able to find relaxation in fishing because the fish will be contaminated. He would not be able to enjoy hunting because the wild fowl and wild animals would be contaminated; and the ocean would fail to be a source of protein because even the ocean would be contaminated.
Dr. Keit Ronald of the University of Guelph said insecticides have reached the antarctic and penguins are being affected. He said the antarctic once was considered to be a sterile part of the world but that it is not any more; it is polluted with insecticides. Dr. Ronald said the day is coming when insecticide will be sold in the same manner as poisons with purchasers signing a poison register.
I support Bill C-157 because it will fulfil some urgently needed controls. Another consideration that should not be overlooked is revealed in a statement by Professor Lamont C. Cole of Cornell University division of biological sciences. He contends that certain pesticides like D.D.T., which can kill both helpful and harmful species, actually make life easier for the pests. He followed that thought with the warning that D.D.T. and other persistent types of pesticides carry perhaps the greatest potential long term hazards to mankind.
The United States secretary of the interior in his reference to pesticides said that we have strained mind and dollar to bend nature to our satisfaction. Yet, we do not know what the effects may be, nor do we anticipate possible consequences. Blithely we carry on our multimillion dollar programs in the pesticide field with wholly inadequate research. We could be building our own fools' paradise. The day of reckoning may not be tomorrow, but who knows about the day after?
At this time I should like to refer briefly to the case at Grand Forks, B.C., more specifically known as Sunshine Valley. The farmers
Control of Plant Pests
there had their hogs, cattle and milk declared unfit for food by the federal food and drug directorate. This was the result of contamination caused by Aldrin which had been used for the control of wireworm in potato crops. It was found that effects of this material remained potent for a long period and would kill wireworm nine years after being administered to the ground. The residue of this chemical was passed on to livestock through forage grown on the potato ground years after being treated with Aldrin.
Much of Sunshine Valley, which is two miles wide by ten miles long, has been rendered useless by contamination. The complete production of several farms has been declared unfit for food. This is a glaring example of a pesticide having been made available before sufficient research work was done so that the end results would be known. In Sweden plans are being made to cut down on the use of insecticides and weed killers to prevent food becoming polluted by chemicals whose long term effects are not known. The Swedish natural science research council which is working on the problem has called public attention to the lack of knowledge available on what biocides do to human beings and whether they can produce cancer. For some time Swedish recommendations discouraged the use of chemicals on food crops during a prescribed safety period before harvest. The period varies from three to 45 days depending on what chemicals are involved. It is calculated to give time for the chemicals to disperse before the plants are used.
The Science council in Sweden now is recommending against spraying. Carrots grown in such soil can contain a higher percentage of dieldrin than the soil surrounding them. Poisons can also enter the human system through eggs. Grain treated with mercury compound has, when fed to hens, produced eggs containing the same substance. The Swedish government now has forbidden the use of dressed seed as feed for chickens.
Bills C-157 supplies provisions that should eliminate some of our pesticide problems. I should like to make a few observations about a product known as Stilbestrol. This material when used in animal food or by pellet implantation has a pronounced effect on the organic function of animals. It is a dangerous product with practically no control. My experiences with this product were disastrous to say the least. As a result of its promiscuous use, damage resulted to a group of mink ranches to the extent of about $750,000. The mink were exposed to Stilbestrol through the

January 14, 1969
Control of Plant Pests
cereal content of their ration which was prepared by a large well-known corporation. Our experience and the experience of others has proven that there is an accumulation of residue in the animal tissues because our mink received a very small amount of Stilbestrol over a period of six weeks following this period, they broke down physically. Many died and practically 90 per cent were sterile.
Further, evidence given by the veterinary general before the agricultural committee indicates that the residue does accumulate. This was borne out by the fact that swine had been declared unfit for human consumption after a residue of Stilbestrol above the point of human toleration had been detected. Thousands of cattle across this country are being fed Stilbestrol. Many also carry Stilbestrol pellets in their ears. I am disturbed about the loose handling of Stilbestrol and its effect on humans who must surely be exposed to its residue constantly. The health of our people should be our first consideration. Therefore, I trust some satisfactory control of Stilbestrol may be exercised through the provisions of Bill C-157. This would possibly help to reduce death by cancer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this bill is timely. Perhaps we should have had the tighter controls which will be possible under this bill even before now. I am concerned about the basis on which the Department of Agriculture will be able to make decisions when it comes to the point of control. One may very well say we will see that some manufacturer may or may not be able to distribute such and such a product, but the important thing really is to know before the product is released what it will do. It is important that there be sufficient staff and sufficient research data so that it may be known what a given chemical product will do. I am a farmer and I know there are chemicals being used by farmers who, as a result of personal contact with them, have ended up in hospital. This is not a general situation but I know products have been sold which can cause rather serious sickness on the part of those who use them if they are careless or if they are get down-wind of these products often enough.
We should be concerned about the effect of these chemicals on human beings. If the Department of Agriculture is to control such chemicals the first thing they must know is what those chemicals will do to individuals who use them and what they will do to the environment in which they are used.

[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
It is quite true that if we were to remove from the market the chemicals which are now being used in agriculture, our agricultural production would drop severely. It is also safe to say that chemicals have been released for use without sufficient consideration as to what they will do to the environment in which they are used. For example, if on the prairies you use a chemical spray which destroys substantial amounts of foliage on the trees, what do you do to the bird population in that area? The bird population is important. If you use chemicals which cut down the ability of honey bees or ordinary bumble bees to survive, what do you do to the insect population and the production of honey in a given area?
The manufacturer is interested in producing a product, advertising and selling it. If he derives a profit thereby he is happy and has achieved his objective. If no one prevents him from deriving this satisfactory profit he is certainly not violating any law, except the law of nature. The law of nature is pretty important because we all live or die by it, as the case may be.
At the moment on the prairies, and I suppose anyplace else, you can use what is called a low volatile spray for spraying weeds, or the standard spray. The low volatile spray will not drift to the same extent the other will. You can use a contact spray for killing weeds or a spray which is taken into the body of the weeds which literally causes them to explode and die. Each one has a different effect on the surrounding countryside and each one varies in respect of the drift aspect.
This is the kind of thing about which the Department of Agriculture should be concerned and I do not think there is enough money or time being spent in this area. Let me give an example in respect of seed treatment. Every spring beginning about March we see a flood of advertising in western Canadian and, I am sure, in eastern Canadian periodicals advising farmers that such and such a treatment should be used on seeds. These advertisements indicate how much is to be used, what a wonderful boon this is if you apply it to the seed, and what you accomplish by the application. I know for a fact that you can get a number of research men in universities together who will argue among themselves as to whether it is worthwhile to use this seed treatment, yet this treatment is advertised and the farmers are urged to use it. This year, as a result of crop conditions,
January 14, 1969



our seed has suffered damage, and we have already seen suggestions from experts and technicians to the effect that we would be well advised not to use this seed treatment at all. In spite of this, thousands of dollars are being spent on advertising to sell this treatment to the farmer. These are the things about which we should concern ourselves.
I am concerned about the basis upon which control is to be established and used. We must consider the actual application on the farm and the general effect of these chemicals on the general environment in terms of water, air and ground pollution. We must not forget that a great deal of this chemical does not simply disappear but becomes a permanent part of the environment into which it is released, whether it is the soil or the water.
Let me urge the Department of Agriculture to concern itself about this aspect and not merely to be satisfied to control what exists or what particular manufacturers choose to offer the public. There are other ways of controlling insects besides dousing them with chemicals. It has been established that insects can be controlled in many cases by biological methods without using chemicals. This alternative method has not been given sufficient attention, and sufficient money has not been spent to develop this method of controlling insects. We continue to douse them with chemicals.

Mr. Speaker, the two preceding speakers have dealt with much of the subject matter with which I intended to deal. This has relieved me of a great burden of responsibility. However, in respect of a collateral issue I think I should make it clear to the house that we have now virtually concluded the fourth bill placed before us today. Contrary to what has been said in some places, these are not unimportant bills. They comprise massive legislation which will have a considerable effect on the lives and fortunes of many thousands of Canadians.
It is of some credit to the house, and to the new basis under which we are proceeding, that we understand that under the new practice we will be following, second reading is not taken to mean an acceptance in principle of what is contained within the four corners of a legislative measure. It is in fact a stage in the legislative process during which we can examine the legislation and then refer it to the appropriate standing committee for examination in depth. If we see fit we can then take issue with the provisions of a bill. I
Control of Plant Pests
am pleased to see that this procedure is being followed.
I know there will be occasions when opposition members and, perhaps hopefully, some government members will be compelled to suggest that certain measures are not good or of advantage to the country. On these occasions, we will feel justified in taking a stand even at the second reading stage. I thought I should make that position clear at this particular time.
At this point I should like to refer to another phenomenon which has come to my mind after listening to what has been said about these legislative proposals. I have in mind the substantial extent to which the government is asking this house to give it the power to regulate by order in council. I do not intend to go into detail, but an examination of the regulatory clause 5 of this bill makes it clear at first blush how very substantial are the rights this house is yielding to the government. This is emphasized by the other bills which have already been passed. I am not going to quarrel about this, but it is a principle I do not like. I think we have gone too far in this direction in the past.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
We have given to the government over and over again, in bill after bill, year after year, parliament after parliament, power to act by order in council and ministerial decree. Our rights then vanish; we do not see them again in this house. The effects of the exercise of rights are of course, felt by people all over this country. I say this because I want to emphasize very strongly the need for a right for this house to examine and scrutinize the impact of ministerial decrees and orders in council.
It is true that a committee has been set up. I had the honour to be a member of that committee. We have not had an opportunity to discuss these matters because we have met only once. I do not fault the committee or the chairman for that. But I urge the government to proceed with all speed to make sure that the committee meets often so that before this session is passed we will have arrived at an acceptable method whereby when we do grant the government, as we are now doing by clause 5 of this bill, the very substantial powers which the minister is seeking, there will be some method of examining, those cases where, in the opinion of members of this house, there have been abuses of the rights given to government.

January 14, 1969
Control of Plant Pests
We are probably the only democratic country at the present time which does not have that right in its legislative assembly. I want to make this point, Mr. Speaker, because I think it is most important. There is no doubt that the government will continue to seek powers of this kind. More and more we will find that bills are simply vehicles from which is suspended the right to pass regulations. There must be given to this house the checks and balances to meet this situation. I make this point now. It is a collateral point but I think I can choose no better time than this to emphasize it.
I shall now deal with the merits of the legislation. I am interested in it. I farmed for some years until I descended into public life. I have some knowledge of what is involved. I had the honour to serve as a member of the health and welfare committee which sat in 1963. At that time there had been recently published a remarkable book by the late Miss Rachel Carson, "Silent Spring". The committee was given very wide powers of reference to examine the impact of herbicides and pesticides on environment, on the human existence. We invited Miss Carson to appear before the committee. Because of ill health she was unable to come to see us, but she sent us some documentation. We had a very full examination of this matter but toward the end of the committee's hearings the representatives of the agricultural chemical industry appeared before it. I am not faulting them. It was a lobby; there is no question about that.
This industry serves a special need. There is some question in my mind whether the special need which it serves is balanced against what may well be the general detriment to society from the use, or I should say the abuse, of these chemicals. In any event, these representatives appeared before the committee and after their appearance the committee made a report which to my mind was a very mild one; it did not go as far as it should have. At the conclusion of the report, the committee said certain things. I will read from the report of the health and welfare committee which dealt with food and drugs in 1963. On page 566, of the report, after making what I consider to be very mild recommendations, the committee said:
The committee finds that it will not be able to complete at the current session of this parliament its inquiries into the matters referred to it for report and, accordingly, recommends that this committee be re-established and appointed early in

the next session of this parliament to resume the studies and continue the inquiries initiated by this committee.
The committee was re-established but it did nothing at all. It decided not to pursue its studies in connection with this very serious problem and turned its attention to other matters dealing with drugs generally. It made some very useful recommendations in that respect, but it did not pursue its inquiries nor has there been to my knowledge any committee since that time which has pursued or even attempted to conclude the inquiries which we initiated in 1963.
We have not heard a great deal about Miss Carson's book, although there has been a subcommittee of the United States Senate sitting under the chairmanship of a very distinguished senator and former governor from, I believe, Connecticut, which has been inquiring into environmental hazards and has made some very useful recommendations and proposed some legislation. I do not think it would do any harm at this time, having regard to the fact that this matter is being referred to committee, to read some extracts from this book to remind the house of the grave dangers pointed out by Miss Carson. In her foreword Miss Carson quotes Albert Schweitzer who said:
Man has lost the capacity to foresee and to forestall. He will end by destroying the earth.
In the foreword to the book there is also a quotation from E. B. White as follows:
I am pessimistic about the human race because it is too ingenious for its own good. Our approach to nature is to beat it into submission. We would stand a better chance of survival if we accommodated ourselves to this planet and viewed it appreciatively instead of skeptically and dictatorially.
I should like to read two other quotations from the book:
We poison the caddis flies in a stream and the salmon rims dwindle and die. We poison the gnats in a lake and the poison travels from link to link of the food chain and soon the birds of the lake margins become its victims. We spray our elms and the following springs are silent of robin song, not because we sprayed the robins directly but because the poison travelled, step by step, through the now familiar elm leaf-earthworm-robin cycle. These are matters of record, observable, part of the visible world around us. They reflect the web of life-or death-that scientists know as ecology.
On page 237 we find these words:
Human exposures to cancer-producing chemicals (including pesticides) are uncontrolled and they are multiple. An individual may have many different exposures to the same chemical. Arsenic is an example. It exists in the environment of
January 14, 1969

every individual in many different guises: as an air pollutant, a contaminant of water, a pesticide residue on food, in medicines, cosmetics, wood preservatives, or as a colouring agent in paints and inks. It is quite possible that no one of these exposures alone would be sufficient to precipitate malignancy-yet any single supposedly "safe dose" may be enough to tip the scales that are already loaded with other "safe doses".
In support of that I should like to tell the house what was said by one of the doctors who appeared before the committee. I tried to find the actual evidence so I could read it to the house, but I could not find it. However, I recall one of the doctors who appeared before the committee being examined on this particular point. He said it will be utterly impossible for 15 or 20 years at least to come to a determination as to the extent to which the constant intake of these pesticide residue may affect the reproductive capacity of the human race.
It may well be-I have not kept up with this-that scientists are now been able to say that this statement is not correct. However, it certainly has not come to my attention and I have tried to keep in touch on with the problem. This was a very serious statement made at that time.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Miss Carsons' critics said that she was an alarmist and was colouring her facts. She was justified in doing so because of the serious nature of this problem. In many cases what she said was confirmed by evidence given before the subcommittee of the Senate in the United States.
I say all this not to oppose this bill but to reinforce the fact that the agriculture committee should take adequate time to resume the study which was commenced in 1963, to examine the further scientific evidence which has now become available, and to see to what extent it might be possible to introduce safety features into the use of these pesticides. I notice that the legislation is substantially different from chapter 209 of the Revised Statutes, The Pest Control Products Act. I should like to call the attention of the minister to the fact that when I was examining the then legal adviser, Mr. Curran of his department, I asked him questions regarding the legal basis upon which the legislative program dealing with pesticides and pest controls had been put forward. It was suggested that, similar to food and drugs, the act was probably based upon the Criminal Code. I do not know whether or not this is the case but I mention it because I think this is another aspect which 29180-2711

the committee may look into, namely the extent to which the wide reaching proposals in the bill and in the regulations are in fact valid. I am not suggesting they are not, but certainly if the government is going to take these powers onto itself it wants to have the utmost assurance that its legislation is in fact valid and constitutional.
I notice for example that for the first time the government is seeking under its regulatory power the right to control the use of controlled products, and this probably comes dangerously close to the regulation of trade and commerce which may or may not be valid. I just throw out this suggestion so that when the committee comes to examine this bill they may call before them the proper officials of the Department of Justice and of the Department of Agriculture and examine these things quite carefully.
I think we must retain the very utmost value that is in the pesticides and herbicides we have developed. At the same time, we must make sure that we do so legally and with the greatest degree of safety to human beings in order that we might have the best of both worlds. I make this plea to the minister to ensure that when the committee examines this particular legislative proposal these things will not be forgotten.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say just a few words on this bill. 1 think it is a bill which has the unanimous support in principle of members in all parts of the house. We agree very thoroughly with the purpose which it sets out to achieve. I believe that the hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Noble), the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) and also the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) have all voiced our real concern that this legislation should be backed up with adequate and continuous research. I think the hon member for Peace River made an excellent suggestion when he said that the committee should go into the whole question of the balance between the good and bad features of these pesticides in the light of the most recent scientific research. I should like to mention an aspect that I do not think has been directly touched upon, that is, not only the whole balance of nature and the effect of pesticides on the plant and animal life but its effect in the home. I think there is a doubt in the minds of a great many people as to the effect a number of these pesticides have on

January 14, 1969
Control of Plant Pests
the deterioration or adulteration of food products.
In my own province there are quite a number of small farms and market gardens which grow their own products without any kind of inorganic or pesticide materials. They believe that when the balance of nature is upset the food products deteriorate. I am not saying that they are correct but I believe we do not know the answer to that, and in order for this legislation to be thoroughly protective we should know the answer to this question. Another matter concerns these compressed air or aerosol containers for destroying pests. I am not at all sure that a build-up of potentially noxious materials does not occur around the home. If the pesticides are not very carefully controlled a build-up may occur which may very well be deleterious to health. This is also something that the committee could and should look into. Before licences are given for the production and handling of these materials producers and distributors applying for registration should be required to show proof of their effects and their controllability.
I am sure that the regulations will have some kind of standards which the producers must meet before being allowed to put their products on the market. I may also suggest that it would be a good idea to require that these pesticides be a genuine improvement on existing ones before the producers are permitted to put them on the market. As is the case with so many food products, in order for a competitor to get the market he often makes some non-essential change in his new product. I think that is something that needs watching. In other words, we must be careful that under this legislation we do not issue licences to permit the slow deterioration or adulteration of foods and of the atmosphere in our homes and cities. We are concerned about the dangers of cigarette smoking and of other products. I believe there are dangers in these pesticides that perhaps we do not even suspect at present. We do not want to issue licences for slow murder by way of pesticides.
So, having said this, I think that all of us are convinced that this is an excellent piece of legislation. I certainly hope that the committee will be able to improve on it and to make sure that all the loopholes are stopped.

The hon. member expressed particular concern about di-ethyl-stiibestrol. The hon. member pointed out that we do not know all that we need to know about the long-term effects of di-ethyl-stilbestrol and other residues, but we are sincerely trying to keep up with developments and amending our regulations accordingly.

INDIAN AFFAIRS-PROPOSED NATIVE TASK FORCE TO DEVELOP POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, late in 1968 representatives of Indian organizations from every province in Canada met to form a National Indian Brotherhood. They met, I think, with the Prime Minister and with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and made a number of proposals to the government. First of all, they proposed that a task force of Indian people be appointed to look into the problems of Indians and to make recommendations for the solution of those problems. They proposed to the government that the government recognize the National Indian Brotherhood as an advisory committee to the government on the problems of Indians. The government, of course, listened as it always does with courtesy, but the answers to the requests of the National Indian Brotherhood were, as usual, to say the least less than satisfactory. Because of the answers that were given to my questions I have risen this evening, Mr. Speaker.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
We hear a great deal about poverty. The report of the economic council says that 20 per cent of our people live in poverty. That is, families of four with an income of less than $3,000 a year are poor. Yet 75 per cent of our Indian people have an average annual income of less than $2,000. In 1963, 47 per cent of Indian families earned less than $1,000 a year. It is not surprising therefore that Indians are dissatisfied with their lot.
We hear a great deal about the lack of adequate housing in this country and we all know of the slums existing in every Canadian city. Yet it is fair to say that most slum dwellers live in palaces when one compares their dwellings with the dwellings of Indians on the reserves. Eighty six per cent of Indian homes are devoid of such elementary facilities as sewers, septic tanks, flush toilets, running water and telephones. I know the minister will tell us that a great deal of money is being spent by his department in helping Indians. But, Mr. Speaker, all that is being done almost exclusively on the advice of


white civil servants and white experts. Almost no Indians have been listened to or consulted in any way on these matters.
Recently the minister was in Winnipeg listening, as he has done in other parts of the country, to the opinions of our Indians with respect to the amendments to the Indian Act which the government has been talking about for so long. If one reads the submissions of the Indians, and I have read them and I presume the minister has given them consideration, one will see how far we are from facing the basic problems of the Indians. They ask that the regulations under the old act having to do with housing and community improvement be amended. Under the old act there were no regulations enforcing minimum housing standards. People talk about educating the Indians. People criticize Indians because their children do not go on to attend high school. I wonder how many white children would go on into high school if they came from a family of six or eight children who had to live and study in a two room house on an Indian reservation. Yet the authorities have never set minimum standards of Indian housing because it has been assumed that Indians are accustomed to and like conditions that are much worse than those that would be tolerated by the rest of the Canadian people.
The Manitoba Indians have asked the government to establish a development fund which Indians could use to develop the resources of the reserve and which would be controlled not by officials of the Department of Indian Affairs and its white advisers but by the Indians themselves. They have also asked for educational facilities to be sharply upgraded, and that this should be done in consultation with the Indian people themselves. I could go on, Mr. Speaker, in much greater detail. A number of briefs have been presented and the briefs have been clear.
One thing which the Indians want more than anything else is their right as citizens of Canada, and surely they are the original citizens of Canada, to direct and manage their own affairs, to make their own decisions and to learn their own mistakes.
We hear a great deal from the present minister. Sometimes we hear the other side from the other minister, the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras), and we wonder who is really running the shop. We have heard a great deal about the subject of listening to the Indians. Yet at the same time the minister
January 14. 1969

proceeded with the reorganization of his department, which instead of decentralizing its affairs centralized them, moving the Indians further away from the decision making than previously. So, Mr. Speaker, I come back to my question of last month. Will the minister really pay attention to the proposals of the National Indian Brotherhood and give the Indians a meaningful role in managing their affairs?

May I ask a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker? May I ask the Minister of Manpower and Immigration whether his representative before the Immigration Appeal Board will take government policy into consideration?
The minister replied:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I give my hon. friend that assurance.
What a kicking around of words! All I was asking was that the government instruct its advocate before that board to make exactly the same point the minister conceded to the parliamentary secretary. But what happened was that no such point was ever made to the board. The counsel briefed on behalf of the Department of Manpower and Immigration did not go before the board and did not say that it is government policy to grant asylum in Canada to those who are political refugees.
Today, I raised the question again with the Acting Minister of Manpower and Immigration to see whether perhaps a government counsel had been instructed, in the light of that exchange briefly on December 20, to change his or the government's tune in the submission to the board in the case of these nine Polish seamen. Most of us know there can be no justification for the alibi that this is a matter which is before the board and therefore the government should stand back.
The fact is the government is represented before that board by a lawyer and the government gave him some kind of instructions to appear before the board. Quite obviously, they have not given this lawyer instructions to present to the board a statement of government policy that Canada in the past has given refuge to people from Communist countries.
I shall conclude by quoting one of the most amazing answers ever given in the House of Commons. It is so amazing that it skipped completely over the head of the fourth estate. This is found in Hansard for November 27 at page 3248 in reply to a written question of mine about illegal Greek immigrants into Canada. I had asked the minister
Did any of the above-
Referring to Greek nationals
-seek refuge in Canada on political grounds and, if so, how many requests were (a) granted (b) refused.


The answer was that no figures are available. If a government department or minister does not know how many people have come to Canada and have asked and pleaded with us to give them asylum because they would be imperiled if they went somewhere else then, sir, it is no government at all.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the honourable member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) for his question. As he mentioned earlier, he asked a similar question on December 20 last which was followed by a supplementary question by the honourable member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) who also shows a particular interest for those Polish seamen seeking asylum in Canada.
We know, Mr. Speaker, that desertion by Polish seamen is not a new thing. These seamen are not the first to desert and ask for political asylum.
In 1966, the department had to deal with seven cases of deserting seamen who wanted to seek political asylum; in 1967, there were 22 such cases and 29 in 1968. The honourable member for Halifax-East Hants said a while ago that the department made a mockery of requests for political asylum. The department does not make a mockery of those requests but the person concerned must give proof of being a political refugee. Until now, there has been no proof that, in the past, deserting Polish seamen, or their families were victims of maltreatment on the part of the government once they had returned to their country. Certain cases were accepted by the department, thanks to a permit granted by the minister.
In this case, the request was turned down by the Appeal Board; some time ago, a new request was turned down and, last week or the week before, a new appeal was made to the board which is due to give its ruling this week. I can assure the honourable member that if the applicants prove to the board that upon returning to their country they will be maltreated or persecuted by their government, the commissioners will grant their request and allow them to become Canadian citizens.
Mr. Speaker, it is a well known fact that Canada, more than any other country, facilitates immigration: proof has been given of this. I therefore fail to see why constant

The subject I wish to deal with is certainly not new to this house. We have brought this matter to the attention of the Department of Transport on many occasions and I am disappointed that there is not a member of the Department of Transport here tonight.
It is my information that about 15 years ago there was a considerable push for a tram-car ferry from Digby to Saint John. Approximately ten years ago a ferry for carrying all kinds of road vehicles was proposed. Approximately six years ago the real push was made, but it was then realized that we might be too late and that south western Nova Scotia had perhaps missed the boat. Since then what have we received? The Princess Helene was replaced by the former Princess Nanaimo, renamed the Princess of Acadia. This ferry that had become obsolete in British Columbia was supposed to be the answer to our transportation problems.
Mr. Regan, the present leader of the Nova Scotia Liberal party, referred to this matter on July 26, 1963 as recorded in Hansard at page 2697. My information is that in 1963 there was almost a firm agreement between the government and the C.P.R. and that only the dots on the "i's" and the crosses on the "t's" had to be accomplished. What has happened since then?
Since 1965 some 22 questions have been asked by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan), all relating to this matter.

The Trudeau announcement of May 30, 1968 related to a multi-million project; a $17 million freight-auto-passenger service. That evening the Liberal candidate was interviewed at a political rally. He indicated that a decision had been made to proceed with the building of a ferry and the terminal this year. That was 1968.

It is a shame, Mr. Speaker, that politics is abused to this extent. There is no patronage, but no boat either, and the people of southwestern Nova Scotia, in the Annapolis Valley, are frustrated, infuriated and depressed by announcements that keep repeating the word "soon". Every time there is political prestige or political headlines to be made, it is the same story-"soon". The Digby Courier of January 9, last week, contained an article wherein a councillor reported to that newspaper that news reports indicated that the tender for the new ferry to run between Digby and Saint John would be awarded soon and that contracts for the terminal would be let in the near future. The same story appeared again last week.
Today I asked a question in the house and received the same answer. What is the secret? Why the sea of secrecy? I say to the government, tell the people, tell the boards of trade, tell the municipal and town governments, tell the M.P.'s and the business people what the hold-up is. What is the problem? Tell us so that we do not have to start anew every time a new government or a new minister is appointed. If the government is not responsible for this and it is the C.P.R. or other agencies that are responsible, why make announcements at all?
It is the responsibility of the government to provide this essential highway link and they should be able to overcome these difficulties. There is an economic future for the Atlantic area but the whole transportation problem must be solved, not only water transportation but air transportation. There is a future for our fishing industry. There is a future for eastern agriculture. There is a possibility of
